# A word to everyone about Glenmore

I’m putting this here on the blog Úna set up all those years ago, because it was meant to keep us in touch, whether we were in Galway or Boston or Perth or Leeds. There are things that ought to be said properly, and to everyone, rather than passed from one phone call to the next. This is one of them.

I have agreed to sell the house in Glenmore, near Oughterard. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it closes on **15 January 2027**.

I want that date written plainly at the start. Some of you already know about the sale, and some have heard only bits of it. Some may be reading it here for the first time. I am sorry I let it happen that way. You should have heard from me before there was anything to hear from somebody else.

I also want to invite everyone who can come to the house on **Sunday 13 December**, before it is cleared. There will be soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies. I’ll say a little more about that below, but please put it in your diaries. I know December is a difficult time to get people together, particularly those abroad, and I don’t expect anyone to do the impossible. Whoever can be there will be very welcome.

Now for the rest of it, which is harder to write.

## Why I have decided to sell

Pádraig Mulkerrin, Tom’s grandfather, built the house in 1931. It was the house Tom grew up in, and for many of you it has been there for as long as you can remember. You didn’t have to live in it to feel that it belonged, in some way, to your own life.

I know that. I haven’t forgotten what the place means because I have signed up to sell it.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It is forty minutes each way. On paper, that doesn’t sound an enormous undertaking. A drive out, a look round, a drive home. I’ve sometimes told myself much the same thing when I haven’t wanted to go.

But keeping an empty house is not just the time you spend inside it. It is remembering what needs checking and wondering what has happened since you were last there. It is knowing that, whether you feel up to it or not, you will have to go again.

I am seventy-one. That isn’t a declaration that I am finished with useful activity, before anyone starts. It is simply one of the facts I have to take into account. I cannot go on maintaining Glenmore, and I have reached the point where I need to say that without immediately offering to manage for another few months.

The roof survey in September made the practical side very clear. Ó Flaithearta’s quoted €38,000 for the slates and the back chimney. That is before dealing with the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing for a sale to anyone anyway.

These are not little jobs that can be put off indefinitely or dealt with by opening the windows more often. I could spend a great deal of money and still be left with an empty house that needs looking after. The roof would be repaired, but I would still be making the journey, checking the pipes and worrying about the next thing.

I don’t want to pretend the decision was only a matter of adding up figures. If it were, it might have been easier. But the figures are real, and so is the work. Loving the house does not make either disappear.

There is another reason, and I have not told any of you about it until now.

Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up.

I know some of you will be upset that I kept that to myself. I don’t have a very good defence. I got up in the end, and I told nobody. That is what happened.

Since then, I have been afraid of being alone at the house. I still go, and I do what needs doing, but I am afraid. I don’t want to keep pretending otherwise just because I have managed so far.

I am not telling you about the fall to bring an end to every objection or to make anyone feel guilty. You are entitled to be sad about the sale, or angry, or both. But if I am asking you to understand my decision, I have to tell you the whole of it, including the bit I would rather have kept to myself.

I cannot keep the house going, and I no longer feel safe there on my own. Those are not things I can put right by waiting until summer.

## Who is buying it

The buyers are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It is not being bought as a holiday let.

That mattered to me.

The price is fair. It is less than the Dublin crowd offered in the summer, and I took the lower offer on purpose. I know people will have their own views on that. I considered it, and I made the choice knowing the difference.

I would rather the house was lived in by a family. I don’t mean that as a grand gesture, and I’m certainly not asking for praise for accepting less money. It was one of the things I could choose, and I chose it.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum.

I have thought about that a great deal. I am not going to put words in his mouth beyond the ones he actually said, or claim that I know what he would say about every part of this. He isn’t here for me to ask. I wish he were.

But he did say that, and the thought of two small children living there means something to me. The house will be their home, with the ordinary business of a family going on in it. It will not be kept empty while I try to preserve everything exactly as it was.

Aoife and Kevin have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. I am grateful to them for that. We will, of course, have to remember that it is their home and be considerate of them. Their kindness is not a reason for us to forget that the ownership will have changed.

Still, I wanted you to know they have said it. Selling the house does not mean we must never set foot in Glenmore again.

## What I am keeping

The house is being sold, but not everything in it is going.

We are keeping the dresser, which is going to Úna’s. We are keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign.

I wanted to put those things down specifically, rather than say vaguely that “the important bits” would be saved. Different things are important to different people, and I know some of you will already have been wondering about them.

The dresser will still be in the family. So will the fiddle. The photographs are coming with us, and the lamp and the sign are being kept. They are not being left for somebody else to decide what to do with.

I also know that keeping a dresser is not the same as keeping the room it stood in. I won’t try to persuade anyone that a photograph is a substitute for being able to open the door of the house. There will be a loss. I feel it too.

But I cannot keep a whole house because there are things inside it I love, or because so much happened there that I want to remember.

Over the best part of two years, I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. I didn’t arrive at that quickly. For a long time the two felt so bound together that even thinking about selling seemed disloyal.

They do not feel quite the same to me now. I can miss Tom in Galway. I can talk about him at Úna’s. I can remember something he said while I am doing something entirely ordinary, nowhere near Glenmore.

The house matters. It always will. But it isn’t the only place where he is remembered, and it cannot be my job to keep it standing empty as proof that I loved him.

## What happened there

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle were watching.

There you are. No lovely sunset, no great privacy. Rain and cattle. I wouldn’t exchange it for a more presentable story.

When I think of Glenmore, I think of that. I also think of the children learning to swim in the lake below the house, and Declan refusing to come out until his lips were blue.

Declan, you may have your own account of how cold you were, but your lips were blue.

Those memories are part of why this is difficult. They are not arguments I have overlooked. I don’t look at the house and see only the roof bill or the damp. I see the place where Tom grew up and where so much of our family life took place.

I know each of you has your own version of it. For some, Glenmore is bound up with childhood. For others, it is a place you returned to from far away, something familiar when much else had changed. I understand why hearing that it is being sold might feel as though a decision has been made about your past without anyone asking you.

I should have made room for those feelings before the sale was agreed. That would not necessarily have changed my decision, but it would have given you the chance to hear me explain it, and me the chance to listen, before it became news.

Instead, I left it too late. Then some of you heard it second-hand, which made something painful worse.

## To Declan, and to everyone who heard that way

Declan heard from Gráinne on WhatsApp, not from me.

That is my fault, not Gráinne’s. I should have spoken to him myself.

He rang me at two in the morning his time. He was very upset, and he said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back that I shouldn’t have said.

I am not going to give an account of the whole call here. It was a conversation between mother and son at a very bad moment, and neither of us needs it turned into something for everyone else to judge. I am mentioning it because it happened, because I know how hurt he is, and because I won’t write a cheerful announcement that pretends there has been no difficulty.

Declan, I am sorry you found out that way. I regret not consulting you. You should have been able to hear it from me and say what you needed to say before I agreed the sale.

I can understand how being told afterwards made you feel that your place in all of this had been disregarded. I am sorry for the things I said when you rang.

I am not angry with you.

But I also need to be clear that I am not willing to wait until your summer visit. The sale closes on 15 January, and I intend to go ahead with it. I cannot keep looking after the house until summer, or keep postponing this because there is never going to be a date when it stops being painful.

I wish I had handled it differently. That is not the same as wishing I had made a different decision.

You don’t have to agree with me before we speak again. You don’t have to arrive at the same view of the house as I have. I would like us to be able to talk without either of us having to win the argument first. The door is open, and I hope you know that.

To the rest of you who heard through someone else, I am sorry too. I should not have left you trying to work out what was happening from a message or a hurried conversation. That is partly why I have written such a long post now. I want the reasons and the dates in one place, in my own words.

## Sunday 13 December

Before the house is cleared, I would like us to have a day there together on Sunday 13 December.

Soup and sandwiches, and wellies if you want to walk. Nothing elaborate.

There is no requirement to come in good spirits about the sale. You can come because you want to see the house, because you want to see each other, or because you would rather have a look round before things are moved. Coming does not mean you approve of my decision.

I would like the day to leave room for whatever people need from it. Some will want to talk, and some may want to walk about quietly. There is no need for speeches. I have probably done enough talking here to cover us all.

If there is something you want to ask me about the house or what is being kept, please ask me directly. I may not have the answer you hope for, but I would rather we spoke than have people wondering.

For those in Boston, Perth, Leeds or anywhere else who cannot make it, I know the invitation does not remove the distance or the expense. Please don’t read it as an obligation. I wanted everyone invited, even those for whom it is not possible.

Let me know if you think you can come, so I have some idea of how much soup is needed.

And, once more, so there is no uncertainty: **the sale closes on 15 January 2027**.

I am sad to be selling Glenmore. I am also relieved that I will not have to go on looking after it. I have found that difficult to admit, but both things are true.

I wish I had told you sooner and done it better. I cannot undo that, but I can be honest with you now.

I hope I’ll see as many of you as possible on 13 December. Bring the wellies, and we’ll put the kettle on.
